title: 82nd Anniversary of D-Day — 29 WWII Veterans Return to Normandy American Cemetery
detail: Twenty-nine World War II veterans attended the 82nd anniversary ceremony of the D-Day landings at Normandy American Cemetery in Colleville-sur-Mer, France, on June 6, 2026. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Gen. Dan Caine, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, addressed the veterans and dignitaries. Caine told the assembled veterans: 'Thank you — thank you for your courage, tenacity and grit that you showed the world on that day, and the days that followed.' Prior to the officials' remarks, 107-year-old Navy veteran Art Rose — an engineering officer at Omaha Beach during the invasion — read aloud a letter he had written to his parents on June 11, 1944, five days after the landings, concluding with an optimistic message that he was 'well, whole and happy.' Approximately 160,000 Allied troops, including 73,000 Americans, landed at Normandy on June 6, 1944, in the largest seaborne invasion in history; an estimated 4,414 Allied troops died on D-Day itself, including 2,501 Americans. The Normandy American Cemetery, overlooking Omaha Beach, contains 9,388 US service member graves. The 82nd anniversary is expected to be among the last at which a substantial group of D-Day veterans, now well into their late nineties and beyond, will be able to attend in person.

title: 30+ Surviving 'Rosie the Riveters' Receive American Spirit Award at National WWII Museum on D-Day
detail: More than 30 surviving 'Rosie the Riveters' gathered at The National WWII Museum in New Orleans on June 6, 2026 — the 82nd anniversary of D-Day — to receive the museum's 2026 American Spirit Award, its highest honor, during the annual Dr. Hal Baumgarten D-Day Commemoration. The women were recognized for powering the wartime industrial effort, learning technical skills including welding, riveting, aircraft assembly, and munitions manufacturing to help produce equipment and supplies for Allied forces while millions of men served overseas. Among the honorees was 101-year-old Delphine Klaput, who worked at the Glenn L. Martin Aircraft factory in Baltimore during the war's final years. This year's American Spirit Award class also included composer John Williams and former NFL player and ALS advocate Steve Gleason. The American Spirit Award recognizes individuals and organizations that 'exemplify the outstanding qualities of the American spirit and inspire these values in others.'
